Search warrants for former prince Andrew's homes were unlawful, UK court rules 
 
  Europe   
 Police who searched the properties of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor as part of investigations into his links to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein have agreed the search warrants were unlawful, a London judge said Thursday. The 66-year-old younger brother of King Charles II was arrested on February 19 on suspicion of misconduct in public office.   
 
 
 
 
Issued on: 08/10/2026 - 16:09Modified: 08/10/2026 - 16:15
    1 min Reading time   
  Share     
 
  By:  
 
  FRANCE 24       
 
     
 Britain's Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew, pictured at Windsor Castle in April 2025. © Kirsty Wigglesworth, AP file photo    
 
British police on Thursday said that search warrants it secured to search properties linked to King Charles III' younger brother Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor had been incorrectly granted and must be quashed. 
King Charles' younger ​brother was arrested on ‌suspicion of misconduct in public office in February and searches carried out at properties in Sandringham, eastern England, and Windsor. 
Andrew was suspected ‌of leaking confidential government documents to the late convicted sex-offender ⁠Jeffrey Epstein when Andrew was a British trade representative, between 2001 and 2011. 
Police have not charged him and Andrew, ​the second son of the late Queen Elizabeth II, ‌has denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein, also saying he regrets their friendship. 
Watch moreEpstein, Andrew's arrest and a royal crisis 
The arrest of Mountbatten-Windsor, and the anger over his relationship ‌with Epstein, left the British royal family facing one of its worst crises in ​90 years. 
Mountbatten-Windsor applied for the search warrants to be quashed and Thames Valley Police said it accepted that they had not been properly granted. 
"We accept the position that the initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed," a Thames Valley Police spokesperson said. 
"Legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation." 
It said its criminal investigation which began after the release of millions of documents by the US Department of Justice relating to the late US sex offender Epstein was still ongoing. 
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

sources.headline: Ex-prince Andrew warrants ruled 'unlawful' as police investigation continues
sources.text:
Published on
08/10/2026 - 21:48 GMT+2
Former prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has won a legal challenge over police searches of his royal residences after officers admitted the warrants were "unlawful", a High Court judge revealed on Thursday.
The court must still decide whether police can keep items seized during the searches. Both the judge and police said the investigation is ongoing.
Judge Nicholas Hilliard revealed on Thursday that police had acknowledged "the search warrants were unlawful".
However, he stressed that "the fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring an investigation to an end", adding that Thames Valley Police (TVP) were continuing their investigation.
Hilliard said he would decide "in due course" on a June legal application by police to retain property obtained under an unlawful warrant "if it would be lawful to seize the property" under a new warrant.
"There would be little point in handing property back if it could then simply be lawfully seized under some other provision," he explained of the police request.
In a statement, the police said they accepted "the initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed."
King Charles III's brother was arrested in February, on his 66th birthday, on suspicion of misconduct in public office linked to his ties with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Mountbatten-Windsor was released the same day after several hours of questioning but remains under investigation. He has denied any wrongdoing linked to Epstein.

sources.headline: Former Prince Andrew files legal action to quash warrants that led to residence searches
sources.text:
FILE - Britain's Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew, looks round as he leaves after attending the Easter Matins Service at St. George's Chapel, Windsor Castle, England, April 20, 2025.
Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP
hide caption
Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP
LONDON — The former Prince Andrew has filed a legal action challenging the warrants that authorized searches at two of his homes earlier this year as British police investigated allegations related to his links to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. A judicial spokesperson confirmed that Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor had filed a claim with the High Court in London and a hearing is scheduled for Thursday.
The Daily Telegraph previously reported that Mountbatten-Windsor had asked the court to determine whether Thames Valley Police acted lawfully in searching the former prince's homes near Windsor Castle and on King Charles III's Sandringham estate. The searches were conducted in February when Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office following allegations that the former prince shared sensitive information with Epstein during his time as the U.K.'s trade envoy. Police questioned Mountbatten-Windsor for 11 hours before he was released under investigation, meaning he was neither charged nor exonerated.
It was the first time in nearly four centuries that a senior British royal was placed under arrest, underscoring how deference to the monarchy has eroded in recent years. Thames Valley Police said Monday that its investigation was continuing, even as it confirmed that the department was involved in legal proceedings about the search warrants. A department spokesman declined further comment while those proceedings are underway. The allegations against Mountbatten-Windsor came to light when the U.S. Justice Department released millions of pages of documents from its investigation into sex trafficking by Epstein and his connections to a network of wealthy, powerful men around the world. Mountbatten-Windsor's relationship with Epstein has been a source of embarrassment to the royal family for more than a decade and forced him to give up royal duties in 2019.
But as further revelations began to leak out of the U.S. investigation last year, the king moved to insulate the monarchy from the fallout by stripping his younger brother of his princely title. After Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested, Charles departed from the "never complain, never explain" approach of his late mother, Queen Elizabeth, and took the unusual step of issuing a statement on the investigation. "Let me state clearly: the law must take its course,'' he said at the time. "As this process continues, it would not be right for me to comment further on this matter.''

sources.headline: Ex-Prince Andrew challenges validity of Epstein-related search warrants
sources.text:
October 5, 2026 / 8:49 AM EDT
/ CBS/AFP
Add CBS News on Google
London — Disgraced former Prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched a legal challenge over search warrants for his royal homes that were issued before his February arrest, Britain's judiciary confirmed Monday. The judiciary confirmed that the U.K. High Court was to hold a private hearing on Thursday, as King Charles III's brother challenges Thames Valley Police over the searches carried out in Windsor, west of London, and Sandringham, in eastern England. The force arrested Andrew on his 66th birthday on Feb. 19 on suspicion of misconduct in public office, related to his links to the late U.S. sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Andrew was released the same day after hours of police questioning, but remained under investigation. He has denied all wrongdoing in his associations with the disgraced American financier.
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, then known as Prince Andrew, Duke of York, is seen in an April 20, 2025 file photo, in Windsor, England.
Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty
His shock arrest prompted Charles to issue a statement insisting "the law must take its course." The Daily Telegraph reported the legal challenge late on Sunday. The newspaper noted it was the first time a member of Britain's royal family has challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649. It said Andrew's legal team wanted to examine whether the search warrants granted by a judge at London's Old Bailey court — formally known as the Central Criminal Court — were lawful.
Andrew's legal team did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment. Andrew's effort to have court "quash search warrants"The judiciary's press office said "the case concerns an application by Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor for a judicial review to quash search warrants issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February 2026."If the review were to throw out the warrants, it would potentially deprive prosecutors handling the case of any evidence discovered during the searches of the former prince's homes.Andrew's arrest and the police searches marked a new low for the royal, who was stripped of his royal titles last year and ousted from his Windsor home over his Epstein connections. The government has even mulled passing a law to remove him from the royal line of succession.
Scandal has engulfed the king's younger brother since one of Epstein's accusers, Virginia Giuffre, claimed in her posthumous memoirs that she had been trafficked three times to have sex with Andrew when she was a teenager. Giuffre died last year by suicide at the age of 41. The former prince has repeatedly denied the claims. He settled a U.S. civil lawsuit in 2022 brought by Giuffre while not admitting liability. The Thames Valley Police probe follows new revelations from documents relating to the American financier released by the United States earlier this year, including emails in which Andrew appeared to share potentially confidential information with him. "Investigation into misconduct in public office continues"In one November 2010 email released by the U.S. government, Andrew appeared to share with the U.S. financier reports on his visit to several Asian countries. Two years earlier, Epstein had been convicted in the United States of procuring a child for prostitution. At least nine British police forces confirmed they were looking into claims — some related to Andrew — stemming from the batch of some 3 million Epstein files released by the U.S. authorities in January.
A police officer on duty at the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk, where Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has relocated following his departure from Royal Lodge in Windsor.
Joe Giddens/PA Images/Getty
However, the Thames Valley investigation appears to be the most advanced. Its officers, who swooped on the remote Sandringham royal estate in eastern England to detain Andrew, searched his home there and his former Royal Lodge residence in Windsor, west of London. The raid in Windsor lasted six days.
In response to Andrew's legal challenge, Thames Valley Police said in a statement that its "investigation into misconduct in public office continues." "We are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained," it added. "As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further."
